power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: This is a methods paper on the physiological interpretation of independent component analysis (ICA) applied to scalp EEG, but its scope extends to historical review and hypothesis-driven research.
First, we trace how the small-patch model, which equates each brain independent component (IC) with a cortical patch smaller than 1 cm², became the central assumption of this interpretation.
Second, we review a clinically and biophysically grounded alternative, the large-patch model (≥ 6 cm²).

The two models make opposing predictions: the small-patch model predicts that about two-thirds of ICs lie on sulcal walls with tangential dipoles, whereas the large-patch model predicts radial dipoles displaced deeper than the cortex because fitting a single dipole to an extended source produces depth bias.
Third, we test them: in simulation, depth bias grew with patch radius and was modulated, but not eliminated, by skull-conductivity mismatch.

In resting-state EEG from two open datasets (820 recordings; 14,578 qualified brain ICs), 77.6% of fitted dipoles lay more than 5 mm inward from the template boundary and 57.9% lay more than 14 mm inward.
The pooled signed-distance distribution showed two prominent peaks, near -1 mm and -19 mm, separated by a pronounced minimum near -5 mm (2-mm bins).
Fitted dipole orientations showed no tangential dominance among deep ICs, which also exhibited higher activation power and lower residual variance than superficial ICs.
These results favor the large-patch model.
ICA remains valid for separating EEG sources, but the depths of fitted dipoles may reflect the spatial extent of the underlying current sources.

(2010) similarly noted that "with the possible exception of early sensory evoked responses, patterns of activation are often sufficiently widespread that the effects of cancellation are relevant to interpretation of EEG and MEG data" (p. 145) (Ahlfors et al., 2010).

text.text: Although combining ICA with a single dipole model is well justified (Delorme et al., 2012), it may give the misleading impression that all ICA-derived EEG sources are Type I. This impression arises because the combination of ICA and single-dipole fitting reduces every source type to Type I in two steps.
text.formatted: Although combining ICA with a single dipole model is well justified <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Delorme et al., 2012)</ref>, it may give the misleading impression that all ICA-derived EEG sources are Type I. This impression arises because the combination of ICA and single-dipole fitting reduces every source type to Type I in two steps.

text.text: First, ICA removes spatial nonstationarity by fitting a time-invariant mixing matrix (Type II to Type I, Type IV to Type III).
Second, the single equivalent dipole removes spatial extent by representing each IC scalp map by a point source (Type III to Type I).
The central hypothesis of the current study is that the spatial extent removed in the second step does not vanish but reappears as depth bias.
Applied to cortical anatomy, the small-patch model makes a specific prediction.
An average gyral crown is only 0.45-0.55 cm wide throughout adulthood (DíazCaneja et al., 2021), so a patch about 1 cm across cannot be accommodated on most gyral crowns.

text.text: In contrast, cortical sulci provide a substantially larger surface: with an average depth of 1.3-1.4 cm and a wall-to-wall width of 0.3-0.4 cm, a single sulcus provides roughly 3 cm of continuous cortical surface from shoulder to shoulder, and the average sulcal length is nearly 700 cm (DíazCaneja et al., 2021).

text.text: Multiple 1 cm² patches could fit within this geometry.
Consequently, the small-patch model predicts a strong dominance of sources arising from sulcal walls rather than gyral crowns.

In this study, we test the two models against each other using ICA-derived equivalent current dipoles and show that the results support the large-patch model, thereby revising the assumptions about cortical source size underlying the physiological interpretation of ICA.
As illustrated in Figure 1, the two models make distinct predictions regarding the depth and orientation of these dipoles.

text.text: The predictions rest on three anatomical facts: only about one-third of the cortex lies on gyral crowns (DíazCaneja et al., 2021; Van Essen & Drury, 1997; Zilles et al., 1988), the average cortical thickness is approximately 2.5 mm, and the average sulcal depth is approximately 14 mm (DíazCaneja et al., 2021; Pakkenberg & Gundersen, 1997; Stark et al., 2007).

text.text: If ICs sampled the cortex in proportion to its surface area, the small-patch model would predict that about one-third of brain ICs are localized to gyral crowns with small dipole angles relative to the radial direction, and about two-thirds to sulcal walls with large angles.
Because a patch about 1 cm across cannot be accommodated on most gyral crowns, the sulcal fraction should be even larger.
In either case, the fitted dipoles should remain within the cortical mantle, where the average sulcal depth is approximately 14 mm.
The large-patch model instead predicts predominantly small dipole angles together with a general depth bias.

Within a patch spanning several gyri, the opposing walls of each sulcus carry dipole layers of opposite orientation whose contributions largely cancel, leaving a net far field approximately radial to the cortical envelope (Ahlfors et al., 2010; Fuchs et al., 2017; Nunez & Srinivasan, 2006).

text.text: When this broad field is fitted with a single equivalent dipole, volume conductor theory predicts that the fitted dipole is displaced deeper than the cortical layer, increasingly so as the patch area grows.

Because this depth bias is known in principle (Ahlfors et al., 2010; Fuchs et al., 2017), we conducted a simple simulation with a four-layer spherical head model, parametrically varying dipole-layer area and depth, to calibrate its magnitude.

Building a forward model To demonstrate the depth bias i.e. the dependence of fitted single-dipole depth on the spatial extent of the true source, we conducted a simulation study using a 4-shell spherical head model.
The radii of the cortex, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), skull, and scalp shells were set to [7.9 8.0 8.5 9.0] cm.
Lead fields were computed using the Fieldtrip function ft_compute_leadfield (Oostenveld et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Lead fields were computed using the Fieldtrip function ft_compute_leadfield <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">(Oostenveld et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Sixty-four electrodes were used, with positions defined by the standard-10-5-cap385.elp montage distributed as a part of EEGLAB library.

EEG sources were defined as uniform dipole layer (UDL) positioned 2 mm below the cortical surface.
The radii of the UDL were parametrically varied (2, 4, 8, 16, 24, 32, 48, and 64 mm), corresponding to surface areas of 0.13, 0.50, 2.01, 8.04, 18.1, 32.2, 72.4, and 128.7 cm 2 , respectively.

In this study, we attempted to determine the physiological interpretation of ICA applied to scalp-recorded EEG.
To this goal, we compared the small-patch source model proposed by early ICA proponents with the large-patch model supported by neurologists and theorists.
Using two European resting-state EEG databases, we analyzed the distributions of ICA-derived dipole depth and their relationships to IC activation power, residual variance, and dipole orientation.
Across these measurements, empirical results consistently favored the large-patch model over the small-patch model.
Below, we discuss the implications of these findings point by point.

The original physiological interpretation of ICA rests on the small-patch source model (Akalin Acar et al., 2016; Cao et al., 2012; Delorme et al., 2012; Makeig et al., 2002; Makeig, Debener, et al., 2004; Onton & Makeig, 2006; Tsai et al., 2014), an assumption that has not been directly tested, although simultaneous EEG-ECoG studies point to larger sources (CosandierRimélé et al., 2007; Ebersole, 1997 Ebersole, , 2000;; Hashiguchi et al., 2007; Ikeda et al., 1999; Kobayashi et al., 2005; Nunez & Srinivasan, 2006; Tao et al., 2005 Tao et al., , 2007)).

text.text: To our knowledge, the present study is the first to explicitly interrogate this core premise and test its predictions against large-scale empirical EEG data.
Notably, despite the widespread adoption of ICA for artifact rejection, its use for extracting putative brain sources has remained limited.

One plausible reason is that the physiological interpretation of ICA critically relies on dipolarity and the associated IDID (Delorme et al., 2012), yet ICA-derived dipole fits frequently yield physiologically implausible depths, which is a pattern supported by the predominance of inwardly fitted dipoles in the present data.

text.text: Specifically, 77.6% of qualified Brain ICs were fitted more than 5 mm inward from the template boundary, and 57.9% more than 14 mm inward.
Although these distances are not directly equivalent to anatomical sulcal depths, the observed depth distribution, together with dipole orientation, challenges the small-patch interpretation.
Such results may have discouraged anatomical interpretation, in addition to the more technical challenge of post-ICA inter-subject inconsistency.
A second reason concerns distributed source models.
Dipolarity is not a physical quantity but a model-relative one: it is the goodness of fit of a single dipole.
It therefore makes sense only within dipole fitting.
Distributed source models applied to ICs provide no equivalent measure, so the validation performed by Delorme et al. (2012) cannot be carried out in that framework.

text.text: Distributed source modeling typically imposes a gray-matter constraint on source locations.
In contrast, our dipole fitting does not impose any constraint on the location of fitted dipoles.

Although the gray-matter constraint is physiologically motivated and computationally useful for solving the inverse problem, it carries the risk of prematurely discarding informative structure present in minimally constrained model outputs.
The present study demonstrates the value of a minimally constrained model by examining outputs that may initially appear physiologically implausible.
As shown in Figure 6 and 7, dipoles localized at implausible depths nevertheless exhibited systematic, spatially organized low-frequency patterns.

text.text: This observation argues against dismissing deep dipoles.

In fact, these deep dipole sources showed higher signal power and lower residual variance, indicating greater dominance and better model fit than superficially localized, physiologically plausible dipole sources.
These observations caution against a bias toward premature physiological interpretation.
Rather, judgment should be suspended (i.e., Husserlian epoché) until the full set of observations can be accounted for in light of basic anatomy and electrophysiology established in the literature.

Finally, the presence of a systematic bias should not be regarded as bad as it may appear because it points to regularity in the underlying generative mechanism producing the error, like the case of the dipole's depth bias we clarified using simulation.
Finally, the present study tested the small-patch model within the methodological framework of the original ICA studies.
We used the same analysis tools and criteria as prior ICA-based work but examined two aspects that have received little attention: dipole depth and orientation.
By applying the original approach to previously unexamined dimensions of the data, we test the small-patch model within its own methodological framework.
Skull-conductivity mismatch in the direction expected for our inverse model would shift fitted dipoles outward and therefore cannot explain the predominance of deep fitted locations.
Our inverse model assumed a BSCR of 80, substantially higher than the value of 27.6 adopted in a recent account of EEG biophysics (Halnes et al., 2024).

Our simulations also produced dipole estimates outside the brain boundary when the inverse BSCR exceeded the forward BSCR, particularly for small patches.
In the empirical data, 1,195 of 2,873 Surface-cortex ICs (41.6%) were fitted outside the template boundary, with a median outward distance of 0.66 mm.

This observation is consistent with the direction of the simulated conductivitymismatch bias, although template anatomy, electrode-position errors, and other modeling uncertainties may also contribute.

text.text: It is a lengthy passage, but because it is central to the argument, we reproduce it in full below without modification.

More formally, we assume that each IC source represents a far-field projection to the electrodes of local cortical field potentials that are fully or partially coherent across a single small cortical domain or patch of unknown size and shape.

In large part because of the extreme preponderance of short-range corticocortical connections (≤100 μm), wholly so for inhibitory neurons and glia, and the predominance of tight radial thalamocortical loops, both supporting oscillatory local field dynamics, models of cortical field dynamics (Deco et al., 2008) demonstrate the emergence of such patches or islands of cortical local field synchrony likened to "pond ripples" by Freeman (2003) and to recurring (point spread) avalanches by Beggs and Plenz (2004).

text.text: Thus, brain connectivity both favors the emergence of temporal synchrony within small, connected cortical domains and minimizes temporal synchrony between such domains other than in exceptional locations and circumstances.

Because of the common alignment of cortical pyramidal cells perpendicular to the cortical surface, spatially coherent local field activity across such a patch will have a non-negligible far field projection to the scalp (Baillet et al., 2001; Nunez and Srinivasan, 2006), forming an effective EEG source whose time course may typically be near statistically independent of the time courses of concurrent far field potentials generated by other, spatially separated cortical source patches.

text.text: Within this passage, the second sentence is of particular importance.
At the same time, it is syntactically dense and conceptually layered.
Focusing on this key sentence, we can simplify the argument as follows:

Because of the preponderance of short-range corticocortical connections (≤100 μm) and the predominance of radial thalamocortical loops, models of cortical field dynamics (Deco et al., 2008) demonstrate the emergence of small cortical patches.

text.text: In the following sections, we refer to this passage as the canonical statement of the small-patch model, and examine its validity.

The small-patch model was motivated by electrophysiological studies conducted at microscopic spatial scales (≈100-1000 μm), including recordings from inhibitory (Budd & Kisvárday, 2001) and excitatory neurons (Stepanyants et al., 2009; Stettler et al., 2002) in the visual cortex of cats and macaques.

text.text: These studies characterized the distribution of cortico-cortical lateral connection distances and emphasized the predominance of short-range connectivity such as ≤100 μm (Delorme et al., 2012) and < 500 μm (Onton & Makeig, 2006).

text.text: From this microcircuit perspective, the original ICA studies inferred that EEG-measurable sources should arise from small cortical patches.

While this inference is intuitively appealing, it overlooks a critical property of population-level field generation that relatively small fractions of synchronized neurons can dominate macroscopic electrophysiological signals.

Empirical and theoretical studies have shown that as little as 1% of pyramidal neurons within a cortical area of 1 cm² can account for approximately 96.5% of the observed signal amplitude (Hari, 1990; Hari et al., 1997).

text.text: This counterintuitive effect arises from the nonlinear scaling of synchronous versus asynchronous contributions in large neuronal populations.

To illustrate this point quantitatively, consider that the human cerebral cortex contains 22.9 billion neurons distributed across approximately 1,883 cm² of surface area in average man (Pakkenberg & Gundersen, 1997; Stark et al., 2007), with roughly 85% being pyramidal neurons (Kanari et al., 2019).

text.text: A synchronized subset comprising just 1% of this population corresponds to 100,000 neurons, whereas the expected amplitude of random, uncorrelated activity scales with the square root of the population size corresponds to 3162 neurons.
Thus, 1% of synchronous neurons can produce 31.6 times larger signal than the background noise.

The underlying simple mathematics shows that the contribution of a synchronized fraction always exceeds that of the entire population acting asynchronously once the number of neurons go beyond a critical mass (0.01 √ , 10000), which is only modest in the spatial scale of EEG (Elul, 1971).

text.text: Independent empirical support for this sparse-synchrony, large-area view comes from the classic work of Walter (Walter et al., 1964).
text.formatted: Independent empirical support for this sparse-synchrony, large-area view comes from the classic work of Walter <ref type="bibr" target="#b109">(Walter et al., 1964)</ref>.

text.text: Using human intracranial EEG recordings, Walter observed that sensory-evoked responses rarely exceeded 30 µV, whereas direct electrical stimulation of the same cortical regions could elicit highly localized after-discharges of 1-3 mV, confined to only a few cubic millimeters of cortex.

Interpreting these after-discharges as an analogue of "fully coherent" activation (as in the canonical statement) of the local neuronal population, Walter inferred that sensoryevoked responses engage on the order of 1% of neurons at any given cortical locus.
The comparison on brain potentials between spontaneous field oscillation and that caused by electrical stimulation was replicated immediately (Cooper et al., 1965).
text.formatted: The comparison on brain potentials between spontaneous field oscillation and that caused by electrical stimulation was replicated immediately <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Cooper et al., 1965)</ref>.

text.text: Walter concluded that:

The conclusion is that a signal from any receptor, even if due to maximal sensory stimulation, can activate only about one neuron in a hundred in frontal cortex, but will have this effect over a vast surface containing several thousand million neurons.

All significant sensory stimuli therefore […] must be considered as activating some tens of millions of neurons over a very extensive area, without necessarily intruding on any other afferent signals or background activity.

The scaling relationship reviewed above implies that scalp-recorded EEG is extremely sensitive to fluctuations in neural synchrony, and that this sensitivity grows rapidly with the spatial extent of the contributing cortical population.
In contrast, the absolute synchrony rate becomes progressively less important as population size grows.

By focusing on micro-scale connectivity and absolute synchrony rates, the small-patch model does not take into account this population-level property of field summation, thereby underestimating significance of the effective spatial extent of EEG-generating sources.

Instead, scalp-recorded EEG is more plausibly dominated by weak neural synchrony distributed across large cortical patches (> 10 cm 2 (Tao et al., 2005 (Tao et al., , 2007)), corresponding to neural populations of > 100 million neurons (Kanari et al., 2019; O'Kusky & Colonnier, 1982; Pakkenberg & Gundersen, 1997; Stark et al., 2007)), with synchrony rate less than a few percent (Hari, 1990; Hari et al., 1997).

text.text: This scaling law is both unique and critical to scalp EEG research, and fundamentally distinguishes it from invasive electrophysiological modalities.
Finally, we found that two anatomical claims commonly cited in support of the small-patch model do not match their sources.

For example, in the canonical statement, work by Deco and colleagues is cited as evidence that an extreme preponderance of short-range corticocortical connections (≤100 μm) supports a small source model.

However, Deco and colleagues explicitly stated that "Intracortical fibers are mostly unmyelinated and extend laterally up to 1 cm (in the human brain) with excitatory and inhibitory connections." (Deco et al., 2008) Their work contains no analysis or claim linking the prevalence of ≤100-μm connections to the emergence of small patches of EEG sources.

text.text: In both cases, the cited source does not support the claim attributed to it, yet these claims have been repeated for more than a decade and continue to reinforce the small-patch model.
We suspect the reason lies in who reads which literature.
The anatomical studies are read mainly by microcircuit physiologists, who have little occasion to open a methods paper on scalp-EEG ICA, and ICA users seldom go back to the primary anatomy.
We have not surveyed the small-patch literature systematically and do not claim that these two cases are the only ones.
Both discrepancies, however, are evident from the cited sources themselves, and readers should consult those sources before relying on anatomical claims passed along through this literature.

text.text: This distinction parallels Walter's separation of specific and nonspecific responses and suggests that scalp EEG preferentially records the extended activity driven by nonspecific thalamic projections.
In Nunez and Srinivasan's terms, the traveling wave is a Type IV source and the extralemniscal projection a Type III source.
ICA reduces Type IV to Type III, and single-dipole fitting then converts the extent of either into depth bias; the present data therefore cannot distinguish them.
How much do sulcal sources contribute to the dominant ICs of scalp EEG?

About twothirds of the cortical surface lies in sulci (DíazCaneja et al., 2021; Van Essen & Drury, 1997; Zilles et al., 1988), yet bipolar, 8-shaped topographies generated by tangentially oriented dipoles were rare among high-quality brain ICs.

text.text: The geometry of an extended source explains this.
When a patch spans a sulcus, the opposing walls carry dipole layers that face each other and point in opposite directions.
Their far fields cancel to leading order, leaving a quadrupolar residual whose magnitude scales roughly with the ratio of the wall separation to the electrode distance.
With the two grey-matter layers 5-7 mm apart and the electrodes 2-3 cm away, this residual is roughly 20-30% of the contribution of a single wall.
The net field of a folded patch is therefore dominated by the radial contributions of the gyral crowns, which sum like a smooth dipole layer on the cortical envelope.
The fundi are also radially oriented but contribute less because they occupy a smaller area and lie about 14 mm deeper, farther from the electrodes. (Ahlfors et al., 2010; Nunez & Srinivasan, 2006).

text.text: In particular, the increase in peak angle across spatial tiers observed under the local-normal reference was not reproduced under the MNI-origin reference.
Neither reference necessarily corresponds to the orientation of local cortical columns.

The present study showed that most ICA-derived brain components yielded deep fitted dipoles (77.6% more than 5 mm inward and 57.9% more than 14 mm inward from the template brain-compartment boundary), without the tangential dominance expected from the small-patch model.
Moreover, the apparent relationship between dipole orientation and depth depended substantially on the geometric reference direction.
Together, these findings challenge the conventional small-patch interpretation and favor the large-patch model as a more plausible alternative.

A lesson from this work is that macroscopic EEG analysis requires a correct understanding of scaling laws: for example, how synchrony in as little as 1% of neurons can outweigh the square root of total but random activity.
ICA itself remains valid for separating EEG sources; what changes is how the depths of fitted dipoles should be read.

We hope that this study motivates future investigations into whether depth bias reflects a general property of EEG source modeling and how such biases may be explained by established and emerging biophysical theories.
